subject: botany_2
question_text: What is meant by plasmolysis? How is it practically useful to us?

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.21, printed question 8. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

insider_note: The question has two halves and the second one is a single line of examples — write the uses even if the explanation runs short, because they are a whole mark on their own.

steps.label: Plasmolysis defined
steps.margin_note: One clean definition sentence plus the name of the state. Three lines.
lines: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplast
of a cell caused by loss of water and turgor.
The cell is then said to be plasmolysed.
steps.why: The definition names the part that moves — the protoplast, not the cell — and that distinction carries the rest of the answer.
common_mistakes: Saying the CELL shrinks. The rigid cell wall holds its shape; the PROTOPLAST inside shrinks.
Leaving out 'loss of turgor'. Turgor loss is half the definition.
steps.memory_tip: The wall stays, the bag inside pulls away.

steps.label: The solution that causes it
steps.margin_note: Name the solution type, define it, and say which way water moves.
lines: Plasmolysis happens when a plant cell is placed
in a HYPERTONIC solution.
A hypertonic solution is more concentrated than
the cell sap.
So water molecules inside the cell move OUT
into the solution.
steps.why: Water leaves because the outside solution has the lower water potential, which is the same rule stated in the water potential answer applied to one cell.
common_mistakes: Writing hypotonic. A hypotonic solution makes the cell swell, not shrink.
Saying the solute enters the cell. It is WATER that leaves.
steps.memory_tip: Hyper means more outside, so water goes out.

steps.label: What happens in the cell
steps.margin_note: Three or four lines naming membrane, wall and the gap that opens between them.
lines: As water leaves, the cell membrane pulls away
from the cell wall.
The protoplast separates from the wall and
shrinks towards the centre.
The space between the wall and the membrane
fills with the outside solution.
steps.why: Naming the two structures that separate is what shows the examiner the mechanism was understood rather than the word memorised.
common_mistakes: Saying the cell wall shrinks. The wall is rigid and does not move.
Stopping at 'water leaves'. The separation of membrane from wall IS plasmolysis.
steps.memory_tip: Membrane in, wall stays put: the gap between them is the proof.

steps.label: Practical uses
steps.margin_note: Two named examples plus one line of reason. This half is a full mark.
lines: 1. Salting of pickles.
2. Preservation of fish, meat and prawns.
Salt or sugar makes the surroundings
hypertonic, so microbes lose water and cannot
grow.
steps.why: The uses all work the same way: raise the outside concentration and the microbes plasmolyse, so the same mechanism answers the second half of the question.
common_mistakes: Listing uses without saying WHY they work. The reason is the mark.
Giving only one example. The question asks how it is useful, so give at least two.
steps.memory_tip: Salt and sugar preserve by making the outside stronger than the microbe inside.
